transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
Two U.S. Senate races are still too close to call, and PR's Ashley Lopez says election
officials in Mississippi and Alaska continue to count ballots several days after the midterms.
Both Alaska and Mississippi have closely watched Senate races that are coming down to very
slim margins. As of Friday at last check, Alaska's Senate race between Republican incumbent
Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola was down to a margin of several hundred votes.
And because the races are so close, every ballot counts at this point. Both states accept
post-mark late-arriving mail ballots, so not all ballots are even at election offices.
Because of the margins, many of those ballots will need to be counted before a race call
is likely, and Mississippi election officials are also working through quite a few provisional
ballots. Those are typically given to voters who face questions about their eligibility
at the polls. Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
What is the fate of Trump administration judicial nominees as Washington moves toward a decisively
Democratic-controlled U.S. Senate? And PR's Nina Totenberg has this look.
With Democrats holding at least 54 votes starting January 3rd, they will run judicial appointments,
quickly until 2030. And among other things, they'll have to decide whether to slow-walk
Trump's judicial nominees, or maybe even block most of them, which Republicans did
in the Obama and Biden administrations, or try to make deals on nominations with the
president. I can tell you one thing for sure, though. If any of the Trump nominees wants
to get confirmed, they will have to answer the question they have consistently refused
to answer at their confirmation hearings, who won the 2020 election?
And PR's Nina Totenberg reporting. President Trump has ordered the U.S. Justice Department
to look into Democrats for, quote, "threatening a lot of people, from officeholders to donors
with impeachment and other forms of punishment." In a social media post without providing evidence,
Trump said that this amounts to a "criminal act." Homelessness in the U.S. saw a major
drop last year, the largest in more than a decade. NPR's Jennifer Ledin reports it was
down for a second year in a row.
The federal housing agency HUD announced the decline of more than 6 percent, and it touted
Trump administration policies, like closing the southern border, as a key factor. Several
cities with big drops had seen an earlier surge of asylum seekers in homeless shelters.
A separate analysis, commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, also finds a
broad decline, says the group's CEO, Anna Levi.
It's good news that more people are getting housed and that the programs that are funded
by Congress are working.
The Trump administration has tried to overhaul those programs, but has so far been blocked
by courts. Despite the latest decline, nearly 700,000 people remain without housing. Jennifer
Ledin, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News in Washington. In Krakow, Poland this afternoon, a gunman opened fire
in the city's busy main square. Six people are dead. Fifteen have been injured. Police
say the gunman was a Polish citizen who targeted random people as he drove through the area.
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a religious cult to 200 years in prison for
the murder of 191 people, most of them children. NPR's Michael Kolokie reports.
The court ruled that Paul Mackenzie, founder of the Good News International Church, bore
primary criminal culpability for ordering his followers to fast to death. Mackenzie
was arrested in 2023 and put on trial alongside 28 of his followers. Prosecutors accused him
and his church of having organized a doomsday sect whose followers were ordered to starve
themselves and their children. Authorities said they found hundreds of bodies in a forest
in the southeast of the country. In a ruling last month, a Kenyan court found Mackenzie
and other co-accused guilty of murder. Mackenzie is also facing terrorism, manslaughter, child
abuse and torture charges in two other local courts. For NPR News, I'm Michael Kolokie
in Nairobi.
A deadline for a new labor contract at the Twin Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach has
been extended through November 20th. The Pacific Maritime Association says talks with the Long
Shoremen's Union will continue over the coming days. The two parties averted a midnight strike
over a contract agreement with Union security guards. The two Southern Californian facilities
handle more than 30% of all of the containerized cargo in the U.S. and ship by truck or freight
rail across the nation. I'm Louise Skivone, NPR News, Washington.
Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks? Amazon Prime members can listen to
NPR News now, sponsor free through Amazon Music. Or you can also support NPR's vital
journalism and get NPR Plus at plus.npr.org. That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races remain too close to call as late mail and provisional ballots are counted
Democrats' 54-seat Senate majority raises questions about handling Trump's judicial nominees
Trump orders Justice Department to investigate Democrats for threatening officeholders and donors with impeachment
HUD reports homelessness fell more than 6 percent last year, the largest drop in over a decade
Gunman opens fire in Krakow, Poland's main square, killing six and injuring fifteen
Kenyan court sentences cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years for deaths of 191 followers
Los Angeles and Long Beach port labor contract deadline extended to November 20 amid ongoing talks
